<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h2 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Gate Semantics</h2><a id="user-content-gate-semantics" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Gate Semantics" href="#gate-semantics"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>Error-level failures cause <code>gate</code> to exit with status <code>1</code>.</li>
<li>Warning-only results still pass the gate.</li>
<li>Successful gate runs exit with status <code>0</code>.</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">This makes ShipCheck useful in CI merge/release workflows, with human review still needed for warnings and release decisions.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h2 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">JSON Contract and Compatibility</h2><a id="user-content-json-contract-and-compatibility" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: JSON Contract and Compatibility" href="#json-contract-and-compatibility"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto"><code>scan --format json</code> and <code>gate --format json</code> conform to the versioned
<a href="/kujolang/shipcheck/blob/7eedd9e02d8730d65e06e16f4984d909d23539bc/schemas/shipcheck-report.schema.json">JSON schema</a>. The schema is part of the
public CLI contract for the current <code>1.x</code> line.</p>
<p dir="auto">ShipCheck makes additive changes to the JSON report only in backward-compatible
releases. Renaming, removing, or changing the meaning/type of an existing field
requires a documented breaking release and a schema-version update. Consumers
should ignore unrecognized fields and rely on the command exit status plus
<code>summary.gate_passed</code> for gate decisions.</p>
<p dir="auto">See <a href="/kujolang/shipcheck/blob/7eedd9e02d8730d65e06e16f4984d909d23539bc/docs/compatibility.md">the compatibility policy</a> for the complete policy,
including the stable compatibility boundary.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h2 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Security and Limitations</h2><a id="user-content-security-and-limitations" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Security and Limitations" href="#security-and-limitations"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">ShipCheck reads repository metadata and invokes local Git commands; it does not
run project tests, inspect release artifacts, call network services, publish
releases, or certify a project. Read the <a href="/kujolang/shipcheck/blob/7eedd9e02d8730d65e06e16f4984d909d23539bc/docs/security.md">threat model and security
boundaries</a> before using it against untrusted workspaces.</p>

Developer Survey 2026

AI

OverviewFull data
View Markdown Open Claude Open ChatGPT

AI moves from on-the-side to built-in

Coding assistants and agents have pulled ahead as the dominant use case for AI (66%), outpacing even general-purpose LLM-powered chatbots (63%). It’s a sign that AI has become less sidekick and more infrastructure, built right into the tools technologists already use. The overwhelming majority of respondents now use coding assistants and agents daily (73%), with nearly a third of daily users spending upwards of four hours.

AI usage

31% of daily AI users use it for 4+ hours/day

Of the over 70% of respondents who use AI daily, 31% use it over four hours per day.
View and share

Despite plenty of societal concern about AI, survey respondents retain a fairly positive view of the technology.

When asked about overall attitude toward AI tools, favorable views outnumber unfavorable ones by almost 3 to 1. But “favorable” doesn't mean “unconditionally positive.” Developers aren't simply handing AI the keys to important decisions. When asked when it’s acceptable to trust AI, 48% indicate they trust AI when they can easily validate the answers and only 16% extend that trust to most tasks that are not important work decisions. The sweet spot where most AI users land is trusting AI when they understand what it’s working on, such as with familiar code (67% currently use AI with this) or when debugging or refactoring (61% currently use AI with this). That’s why human-in-the-loop is the dominant mode of working with these tools.

“This is where I personally feel the importance of human judgment. If you leave it up to chance, if you leave it up to the roll of the dice of the LLM, you're not gonna get the specificity. Everything I've been doing and everything my team's been doing is imagining AI as an exoskeleton, like a Tony Stark augmentation, as opposed to an empty Ultron with nobody inside. Which nobody wants.”

Scott Hanselman, VP of Developer Community at Microsoft

The right tool for the job

The same caution shows up in how people choose (and choose against) certain tools. Developers switching to new AI tools are doing it mostly because the output is better (25%) or because their organization required it (11%).

AI at work

25% switch AI tools due to better output quality

Seeking superior output quality is the single largest reason developers switch AI tools, though a third (34%) retained their original tool choices over the past year. For all the concerns over token costs, only 6% switched because of costs.
View and share

What are they using? Claude Code (66%) and GitHub Copilot (59%) are the leaders for coding agents. Respondents are using LangChain (30%) and OpenAI Agents SDK (24%) for orchestration and Make (39%) and n8n (33%) for automation. AI memory and agent orchestration tools show a notable gap between current adoption and stated interest, suggesting that the category is still finding its footing. Coding agents, meanwhile, are a more mature market with clear leaders emerging.

That selectivity becomes very clear once you look at where AI is actually being put to work. Basically, developers trust AI with machines but not with people. AI use is common, and commonly accepted, across code generation, debugging, testing, and understanding unfamiliar codebases. Even secondary review functions—analyzing telemetry, reviewing pull requests, hunting for security issues—are seeing meaningful AI adoption.

The human difference

But the moment the task shifts toward human communication or creative output—writing emails, generating multimedia, anything requiring a feel for what people want—usage falls off a cliff. The same split shows up in perceived usefulness: technical tasks like implementation and debugging are both useful or very useful to 70%+ of survey respondents, while communication and design lag behind, landing in “slop” territory with 35% and 49% respectively finding AI useful or very useful in those areas.

The top 5 tasks that respondents are currently using AI or AI agents for
The inevitable takeaway is that technologists see AI as very good at technical problems with checkable answers, and considerably less good at solving the other everyday problems of work. A significant chunk of respondents who avoid AI completely do so out of concern for their own skills, privacy, or the technology’s enormous ethical and environmental footprint.

AI at work

6 out of 10 users cite a reason to avoid using AI at work or school, losing job skills is a top concern.

<span data-as="p">Persistence lets LangGraph applications keep useful information beyond a single graph run. It matters when an agent needs to continue a conversation, resume after an interruption, recover from a failure, or remember information across interactions.</span>
<span data-as="p">LangGraph provides two complementary persistence systems:</span>
<ul>
<li><strong><a href="/oss/python/langgraph/checkpointers" class="link">Checkpointers</a></strong> persist a thread’s graph state as checkpoints. Use them for short-term, thread-scoped memory, including conversation continuity, human-in-the-loop workflows, time travel, and fault tolerance.</li>
<li><strong><a href="/oss/python/langgraph/stores" class="link">Stores</a></strong> persist application-defined data outside the graph state. Use them for long-term, cross-thread memory, including user preferences, facts, and shared knowledge.</li>
</ul>
<span data-as="p">Most applications can use both: a <a href="/oss/python/langgraph/checkpointers" class="link">checkpointer</a> tracks the current thread, and a <a href="/oss/python/langgraph/stores" class="link">store</a> tracks durable information across threads.</span>
